title: Written standards, enforced
asks: The organization writes down what it expects of the people who run the system and holds them to it.
how: A written list of lines the site never crosses is enforced in code: every outbound channel runs the same check before anything is sent, and a test keeps the written list and the code in step.
gap: Nobody signs an acknowledgment of the standards.
solo: The only person bound by the standards is the person who wrote them, so an acknowledgment would be a signature on one's own memo.

title: Roles, background checks and training
asks: Reporting lines and roles are defined, people with access are screened, and everyone takes security training when hired and every year after.
how: None of this exists in a form an auditor could test. There is one person: no org chart, no hiring process, no training record.
gap: An org chart, a background check, and a dated training record, even for a company of one.
solo: An auditor will still test the one person against these criteria. The fix is paperwork rather than code: a written role, a screening record and an annual training certificate.

title: A current description of the system
asks: The organization knows and documents what the system is, where its boundaries are, and who can reach what.
how: A written threat model names every kind of actor, what each can reach and what bounds it. A public system map shows the parts and how they connect.
gap: The threat model was last verified on July 4, 2026. Nothing schedules the next review.

title: Telling users what is happening
asks: Users are told about the system's commitments and about incidents that affect them.
how: A public status page reports each component as up, degraded or down, from a health check every three hours, and a privacy page lists what the site stores in a visitor's browser.

title: A risk assessment that repeats
asks: Risks to the system are identified and analyzed, and the assessment is repeated as things change.
how: The threat model names its known gaps instead of hiding them, and the one path that merges code without a person has its remaining risk written down and accepted.
gap: The assessment was written once. There is no second one to show that it repeats, and no calendar that makes it.
evidence: docs/capabilities/08-security-privacy-resilience.md#Named here as the gap rather than; docs/capabilities/06-automation-and-ops.md#residual risk

title: Checking that the controls still work
asks: The organization evaluates whether its controls are present and functioning, and acts on what it finds.
how: Every scheduled job is listed in a catalog that a test keeps in step with the real schedules, and a dashboard sorts each job into fired, failing or silent.
gap: The scheduled jobs were all switched off from July 29 to October 8, 2026 to cut the monthly bill, so the dashboard has a gap in its record for that period. They run again now, but a few stay off on purpose.

title: Policies deployed as tests
asks: Control activities are put in place through technology and through written policies that people follow.
how: Policies here are tests that run on every change: the credential inventory, rate-limit coverage, the boundary around client records, the lines the site never crosses. The build fails if any one of them breaks.

title: Least-privilege access
asks: Access to information and systems is limited to what each person or process needs.
how: Access is an ordered ladder: none, view, edit, admin. A member of a shared board sees only that board, and an unknown board and a board you are not on both answer "not found". Automated agents act only through tokens scoped to a grant.

title: Reviewing who has access
asks: Access is granted through a process, removed when it is no longer needed, and reviewed on a schedule.
how: Grants are recorded, and every use of an agent's access token is written to an audit log. But nobody reviews the full list of who can reach what on a schedule.
gap: A dated, recurring access review with a record of what was removed.
solo: The reviewer and the person whose access is being reviewed would be the same person.

title: Credentials encrypted and accounted for
asks: Credentials that protect the system are themselves protected.
how: Stored credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, changed from an admin screen without a redeploy, and every change is logged. A test fails when code uses a credential the ledger has never heard of.
gap: Keys are rotated when someone decides to, not on a calendar.

title: Protecting the edges
asks: The system is protected against threats from outside its boundaries.
how: Every route that writes data must be rate-limited, gated behind sign-in, verified by a signature, or listed with a written reason. A test fails on any new route that is none of these. Inbound webhooks are checked with a constant-time comparison.
gap: The rate limiter keeps a separate count on each server instance, so a caller spread across instances gets more than the limit. The security doc says so.

title: Encryption in transit
asks: Information moving between the system and its users is protected.
how: Every response tells browsers to use HTTPS only, for two years, subdomains included.
gap: There is no full Content Security Policy. The config explains why one was not added blind.

title: Finding vulnerabilities
asks: The organization detects new vulnerabilities and unauthorized or malicious software.
how: Nothing scans for them. No automated dependency updates or vulnerability scans are configured, and the install step in CI skips npm's own audit.
gap: A dependency scanner on every pull request, and a record of what was found and fixed.

title: Noticing when something breaks
asks: The system is monitored for anomalies that could mean an attack, an error or an outage.
how: Errors go through one reporting function. A watcher compares the live deployment with the latest commit and alerts when production stalls, and it runs off the hosting provider so it still fires during that provider's outage.
gap: Both watchers run on schedule, but the health check looks every three hours and the deploy watcher twice a day, so an outage can go unheard for hours. Every alert reaches one person, and nobody else is watching when that person is away.

title: Responding to incidents
asks: Incidents are evaluated and contained, then fixed, and the lessons are written down.
how: A failed check opens an incident, which moves through one state machine until it is resolved, and alerts page the operator by Telegram.
gap: There is no written response plan and no postmortem convention. The security doc names the missing convention as a gap.

title: Every change tested and approved
asks: Changes to the system are authorized and designed, then tested and approved, with a record kept, before they reach production.
how: Every change lands through a pull request that must pass lint, the full test suite and a build that matches production. One narrow path merges small agent-written fixes without a person, and it fails closed.
gap: Nobody but the author approves a change. The one automated reviewer was switched off when its API budget went to zero.
solo: Separation of duties needs a second person: whoever writes a change should not be the one who approves it.

title: Vendor risk
asks: Risks from vendors and business partners are assessed and managed.
how: The credential ledger names every outside service the site holds a key for, so the vendor list is complete and a test keeps it that way.
gap: Nobody collects the vendors' own SOC 2 reports or writes down a review of them.

title: Backups that restore
asks: Data is backed up, and recovery is tested.
how: A weekly job dumps the business-critical tables, encrypts the archive, copies it offsite, then restores it into a scratch database and checks the rows, because a backup that cannot restore is not a backup. A runbook sets recovery targets for each zone. Portfolio OS, the business record, has its own nightly encrypted export and restore test, and records each result.
gap: The job was paused from July 29 to October 8, 2026. Since the schedule came back, every weekly restore test has passed, six in a row from October 11 to November 15. A Type II period is usually three months or more, so the record is real but still short.

title: Capacity and cost limits
asks: Capacity is managed so the system can meet its commitments.
how: AI spend is logged on every call, and a brake stops paid calls at the monthly ceiling before a runaway bill can take the service down. Public endpoints are rate-limited.

title: Confidential records walled off
asks: Confidential information is identified and protected.
how: A client's records can be imported only by that client's own module. A test scans the codebase and fails if anything else reaches in, and it also fails if it scanned too few files to mean anything.

title: Disposal on a schedule
asks: Confidential information is disposed of when it is no longer needed.
how: A written retention policy deletes dinner-guest replies 30 days after the event and retires stale scraped listings, and unclaimed anonymous boards are deleted after 30 days.
gap: The mail inbox declares a retention period it does not enforce. The deletion sweeps run again as of October 8, 2026 after a pause since July 29.

title: Accurate processing
asks: Inputs and processing are complete and accurate.
how: Money is stored as whole cents, never as floating-point dollars. Published figures are recomputed on every change. Payment webhooks are accepted only with a valid signature.

title: Notice and choice
asks: People are told what personal information is collected and are given choices about it.
how: A privacy page lists every cookie the site sets. The one optional analytics cookie stays off unless the visitor accepts it.
gap: The notice covers the browser. It does not describe the personal information held in the private household and client tools.
